source_text: Praestructio superioris epistolae ita duxit, ut de titulo eius non retractauerim, certus et alibi retractari eum posse, communem scilicet et eundem in epistulis omnibus. quod non utique salutem praescribit eis, quibus scribit, sed gratiam et pacem, non dico: quid illi cum Iudaico adhuc more, destructori Iudaismi? — nam et hodie Iudaei in pacis nomine appellant et retro in scripturis sic salutabant — sed intellego illum defendisse officio suo praedicationem creatoris: quam maturi pedes euangelizantium bona, euangelizantium pacem. euangelizatur enim bonorum, id est gratiae dei pacem, quam praeferendam sciebat. haec cum a deo patre nostro et domino Iesu adnuntians communibus nominibus utatur competentibus nostro quoque sacramento, non puto dispici posse, quis deus pater et dominus Iesus praedicetur nisi ex accidentibus, cui magis competant. primo quidem patrem deum praescribo non alium agnoscendum quam et hominis et uniuersitatis creatorem et institutorem; porro patri etiam domini nomen accedere ob potestatem, quod et filius per patrem capiat; dehinc gratiam et pacem non solum eius esse, a quo praedicabantur, sed (et) eius, qui fuerit offensus. nec gratia enim fit nisi offensae nec pax nisi belli.
pass_a_gloss: The introduction to the previous epistle led in such a way that I did not reconsider its title, certain also elsewhere it can be reconsidered, namely common and the same in all epistles. Which not certainly prescribes salvation to those to whom he writes, but rather grace and peace, I do not say: what does he have to do with the Jewish custom, still destroyer of Judaism? — for also today Jews call in the name of peace and previously in writings thus greeted — but I understand he defended by his duty the preaching of the creator: which the swift feet of the evangelizers of good, evangelizers of peace, bring. For peace of the good, that is of the grace of God, is evangelized, which he knew to be preferable. These things, since announcing from God the Father and Lord Jesus with common names suitable to our sacrament also, I do not think can be despised, who God the Father and Lord Jesus is preached unless from accidents, to whom more are suitable. First, indeed, I prescribe the Father God not another to be recognized than the creator and institutor of man and the universe; further, the name of Father also to come to the Lord on account of power, which also the Son receives through the Father; then, grace and peace not only to be of Him from whom they were preached, but also of Him who was offended. For neither is grace made unless of offense, nor peace unless of war.

pass_b_english: The introduction to the previous epistle led me not to revisit its title, since I am certain it can be examined elsewhere—common, namely, and the same across all epistles. It does not simply prescribe salvation for its recipients, but grace and peace. I do not ask: what business has he with the Jewish custom, he who is the destroyer of Judaism?—for even today Jews invoke peace by name, and formerly they greeted one another that way in the Scriptures—but I understand that he was defending, as his duty required, the preaching of the Creator: the very message that the swift feet of the evangelizers of good, the evangelizers of peace, bring. For the peace of the good—that is, the grace of God—is what is evangelized, and he knew it was to be preferred. Since he announces these things from God the Father and Lord Jesus, using common names that also fit our sacrament, I do not think it can be despised—unless someone preaches God the Father and Lord Jesus only from their incidental attributes, to which those attributes more properly belong. First of all, I prescribe the Father as God, recognizing no other than the Creator and Institutor of man and the universe; furthermore, the name of Father also accrues to the Lord on account of power, since the Son also receives it through the Father; then, grace and peace belong not only to Him from whom they were preached, but also to Him who was offended. For neither is grace made except from offense, nor peace except from war.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal gloss, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances, including the causal relationship in 'quod et filius per patrem capiat' and the conditional/exception logic in 'nisi ex accidentibus'. Scripture references in the Latin (retro in scripturis) are handled correctly as a general allusion in the English.

The Latin text is accurately translated in both Pass A and Pass B. The title 'Introduction to Previous Epistle' correctly reflects the content of the passage. All key terms and concepts are preserved, including theological distinctions and scriptural allusions. No errors in citation, negation, agency, or doctrine are present.
